item.content:encoded:
I really like it. It makes perfect sense to me for the foundation to consider music a memetic hazard, because that is literally exactly what it is.

Music is nearly the exact definition of a meme, in it's original non-SCP meaning. And an anomaly is just something that deviates from normal behavior.

Rock and Roll, experiencing an unprecedented level of popularity and influence IS anomalous, and it IS memetic. It's simply not supernatural. But given how difficult that would be to prove in many instances, it is easy to understand how someone could come to the (flawed) conclusion that it was, especially if they live a life as isolated from normal social trends as the O5 presumably do.

item.content:encoded:
There's a line between a simple psychological effect, and an effect that acts anomalously on listeners. The trouble is where is that line drawn? If I have a CD recording that attempts to hypnotize listeners and plant suggestions to buy more popcorn, is it anomalous or just a bad marketing gimmick? (I'd wager it would probably depend on how effective it was.) If the Foundation was ran by folks with similar leanings as those that wanted to ban rock because of its "corrupting influence", then it's likely that line was placed a bit too far on the wrong side.

In this case specifically, I can easily see someone equating the phenomenon that was happening that matched perfectly with an earlier case file without researching too deeply into it, and the secrecy involved insured that it wasn't properly peer reviewed.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is taking a concept that was, in the real world, considered to be a drastic aberration from the norm, either some congenital defect or an actual, communicable disease. This is fact. It had nothing to do with "being a stuffy prude being the rage", it had everything to do with the fact that the societal norm was to shove anything to do with intimacy into the closet; carnality and kink existed, it always has and always will, but it was DEEPLY buried and practiced with giggling naughtiness (or self-hating vindication) where nobody would ever see.

This article is written in the tone of a group (the Foundation, or an antecedent thereof) reacting to what is perceived to be a sporadic, inexplicable abnormality. As science and understanding marched on, it became obvious that this occurrence was neither, simply something that had not yet been understood. THAT IS THE ENTIRE POINT, it USED to be bizarre and unexplained, but it no longer is.

Who knows? Maybe in a hundred years, we'll find whole colonies of http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-131 and figure out how they work and they're actually perfectly natural. Maybe some of the "undefinable materials" of various things will be examined using new sciences, defined, and no longer be considered anomalous. But since these are all fictional things on the website, maybe there will be an -EX made involving this insane compulsion spread through the internet, underlying causes will be found out, and a charming "public information" acronym will be formed, like… G.I.F.T.?

The O5 are the leaders of the Foundation, but they aren't kings whose word is law. In my headcanon, the Foundation has some sort of constitution or organizational charter that sets rules for what they can and can't do (like no contact with SCPs for instance). Part of the Ethics Committee's job is to be sort of the "Supreme Court" of the Foundation and enforce those rules.

In the rare case that an O5 should go rogue, or become affected by an SCP, or spend 40 years using a poorly researched SCP from the 19th century to justify a social engineering campaign, the Ethics Committee would have the power to "ask" that O5 to step down. I imagine the criteria for authorizing it is pretty steep, like impeaching the president - probably a unanimous vote and the consent of at least two other O5 members.
